bib.title: Before you model: Planning and scoping a project (chapter 3 of Machine Learning Engineering in Action)

question: How should an ML team plan, scope and time-box research and experimentation with the business before building models so projects meet business needs?
hypothesis: Planning and scoping failures, not algorithms or data, are the biggest killers of ML projects; communication-first, time-boxed, demo-heavy work reduces rework.

limits: Evidence is the author's anecdotal experience and an intentionally hyperbolic composite scenario (he says so), not measured studies.
Time-box lengths (1-2 weeks, 2+2 weeks) are rules of thumb; he states no standard rubric exists.
Survey statistics in Fig 3.8 are 2020 secondary figures with unclear per-statistic attribution.
Author gives no year or publisher details in the chapter PDF; the book's date is not printed here.
practices: Open the first meeting with 'Why are we building this?' to define expectations, the performance metric and production attribution score (3.1.1, p.48).
Keep the 'how' (algorithms) out of meetings with the business; discuss it later inside the DS team (3.1.2, p.53).
Ask SMEs 'how do you do this now' and have them show it; this surfaces critical features and business rules (3.1.2, p.54-56).
Validate data with quick statistical reports and SME questions before modelling, e.g. unique product counts per category (3.1.1, p.52).
Do not rely on error metrics alone; supplement with end-use simulation reviewed by SMEs (sidebar, p.47).
Present cost (time, money, people) of requested additions and let the internal customer decide (p.52).
Explain results in abstract, layperson terms to avoid the curse of knowledge (p.52-53).
Plan frequent demos per critical feature; a slide deck or wireframe mock-up is enough, not a built front end (3.1.3, p.56-58).
Cull experiments early; do not run parallel full bake-offs to MVP (3.1.4, p.58-60).
Time-box research and experimentation, and tell the business how long it will take (3.2.1-3.2.2, p.62-63).
Narrow candidate approaches to two or three heterogeneous options and rate each for risk and time to implement (Fig 3.12, 3.16).
Prototypes should balance speed and comparability, with no tuning and no production-quality code; share a static materialised dataset across teams (3.2.3, Fig 3.14).
Estimate development time and total cost of ownership (ETL, retraining frequency, platform, serving, storage) at the end of experimentation (p.71).
Choose among prototypes with a weighted decision matrix where an unbiased reviewer sets ratings and the team debates weights (Fig 3.18, p.73-74).
Guard against owner bias: prefer a boring, similar-quality solution; ask an uninvolved peer to draft the comparison (p.74).
Do not learn new technology on a business project when a familiar solution works (p.73).
Plan but keep plans flexible, consistent with Agile (sidebar, p.43).
Prefer the simplest approach that solves the problem (p.41, 53, 69).

terms.definition: Setting expectations and time boundaries for the research and experimentation phase, distinct from scoping the build.
Business leadership assumes the ML team knows aspects of the business considered widely held knowledge.
Teams assume data is clean without validating it.
Business assumes expected behaviours (e.g. not recommending a just-bought item) without stating them.
ML team goes into technical detail the audience cannot follow; covered further in chapter 4.
Without planning, the team experiments on many state-of-the-art approaches and loses focus on the project's point.
Taking on added complexity for the team's own motives without clear gain.
Over-choice: an overabundance of options is paralysing; Tyranny of Small Decisions: many small choices accumulate into an unfavourable outcome.
Daily run cost to retrain models, generate inferences, host and serve the data, plus maintenance.
Latching onto a clever solution simply because you built it.
